newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl starts jobs pact for east Germany.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl starts jobs pact for east Germany.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday launched a "jobs pact" with trade unions and business to create 100,000 new jobs a year in the former communist east, still blighted by unemployment seven years after unification.
"This is an important day for the new (eastern) states and Berlin," Kohl told a news conference to launch the joint pact.
"This is a good signal for the development of east Germany, for the future of the whole of Germany as a place to do business and also a clear signal of readiness to cooperate."

Kohl, who promised east Germans an economy with "blossoming landscapes" after unification in 1990, is anxious to bolster their faith in his government in the face of 17 percent unemployment and weak economic growth.
"Many people in the east feel repelled, unjustly treated and like second class citizens," Dieter Schulte, head of the German Federation of Trade Unions, told the news conference.
"The goal of all these measures is to improve and equalise living standards."
Opposition parties welcomed the pact but said the participants now had to turn rhetoric into action.
"The initiators still have to prove that the initiative is more than just help for Helmut Kohl's election campaign," Greens board spokeswoman Gunda Roestel said in a statement.

The pact came a day after Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt launched a new investment support package for the east to offer specifically-targeted investment grants rather than the existing tax depreciation incentives which have often led to investments being seen as having dubious value.

The package would initially keep investment support at constant levels but Rexrodt said it would cost around half as much by scrapping generous tax write-offs now available to investors in the region.

Kohl said he was sure the package, set to cut the burden on the annual budget from a current 11 billion marks ($6.5 billion) to 5.7 billion marks in 1999 and to 4.4 billion after 2002, conformed to European Union regulations.

Wolfgang Thierse, deputy leader of the opposition Social Democrats, said the package represented a significant cut in support. "The government is further saving on development of the east at a time when the distance between east and west is increasing both economically and socially," he told Berlin radio.
The investment package and jobs pact came as two economic institutes published reports predicting further economic stagnation in the east.

The German Economics Institute in Cologne said few east German firms expected improvement in growth, employment or investment. Munich's Ifo institute said eastern firms were less optimistic in April than in March.

The new jobs plan aimed to bring unions, politicians and industry together to reach non-binding agreements on job creation measures, training and investment in a forum likely to be similar to the Kohl's pet "Alliance for Jobs" that collapsed in acrimony just over a year ago.

Hans-Peter Stihl, president of the Federation of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce, said the initiative showed business wanted to boost development in the east, where productivity is only 57 percent of the level in the west.
Industry sought to stabilise investment at levels that allowed above-average growth, boost consumption in the east by 50 percent by 2000 and help new businesses, he said.

Manfred Stolpe, premier of the eastern state of Brandenburg said the initiative was necessary because unemployment threatened social peace. "This is not about election chances in coming years, but about the future of our whole fatherland."
